Around 250 BCE the Buddhist monk Mahinda travelled from India to Sri Lanka and converted King Devanampiya Tissa of Anuradhapura. Sri Lankan tradition says he was the son of the Indian emperor Ashoka, sent as one of several missions after the Third Buddhist Council.

The chronicles tell that Mahinda met the king while he was out hunting on the hill of Mihintale, tested his wit with riddles and then preached to him. The king and his court accepted the teaching. The event is still celebrated each year at the June full moon, the Poson festival.

The king gave Mahinda a royal park in the capital, where the Mahavihara monastery grew up. Mahinda's sister Sanghamitta followed, founding the order of nuns. She brought a cutting of the tree at Bodh Gaya under which the Buddha was awakened. The tree grown from it, the Sri Maha Bodhi, is still alive and is said to be the oldest planted tree with a known date.

Sri Lanka became the stronghold of Theravada Buddhism, the "teaching of the elders". Its monks wrote down the Pali Canon in the 1st century BCE and kept the tradition when it faded in India. From Sri Lanka, Theravada later spread to Burma, beginning at Pagan, and to Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.
